text: A cognate is a word that looks and sounds alike in two languages because both come from the same older word. English took thousands of words from French after the Norman Conquest in 1066.

parts.heading: Spelled exactly the same

parts.heading: Almost the same

body.line: How a silent letter links to the next word, and why it changes what you hear.

parts.heading: Silent letters at the end
parts.note: Final s, t, x and d are usually silent. The plural s is silent too, so {ami} and {amis} sound the same. A final r or l is often heard, as in {bonjour} and {il}.
text: Most consonants at the end of a French word are silent. You write them, but you don't say them.

parts.heading: Words that run together
parts.note: The silent s at the end of {les}, {vous} and {ils} turns into a z sound before a vowel.
text: Many French words end in a letter you do not say. When the next word starts with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u or a silent h), that letter wakes up and links the two words. This link is called liaison.

parts.heading: With and without
text: Hear each pair without the link, then with it. Without it, the words blur into one. With it, you can hear each word.

parts.heading: A link can change the meaning
parts.note: In {ils sont}, the s sound belongs to {sont}. In {ils ont}, the z sound is carried over from the end of {ils}.
text: {ils sont} means they are. {ils ont} means they have. The only sound that tells them apart is s or z.

parts.heading: More to hear
parts.note: You do not need to work it out each time. Copy what you hear, and the links come with practice.
text: The same link, in words you know.

parts.heading: Elision: {l'ami, j'ai}
parts.note: A silent h counts as a vowel, so {homme} takes {l'} as well. The same happens to {si} before {il} in {s'il vous plaît}. Elision and liaison work together. One friend is {l'ami}. More than one is {les amis}, where {les} keeps its s and links with a z sound.
text: Before a vowel sound, {le}, {la} and {je} drop their vowel and take an apostrophe. The two words then sound like one.

blocks.definition: Say ten, then the number: 17 is ten-seven.

blocks.definition: Learn the tens, then add the numbers 1 to 9 after them.
blocks.example: {vingt} (20), {trente} (30), {quarante} (40), {cinquante} (50), {soixante} (60)

blocks.definition: Put '{et}' between the ten and '{un}'. From 2 to 9, join them with a hyphen. Before a feminine noun, 'un' becomes '{une}', as in '{une voiture}'.

blocks.definition: French says 70 as sixty-ten, then counts on with 11 to 19: sixty-eleven, sixty-twelve, up to sixty-nineteen. 71 keeps '{et}': '{soixante et onze}'.

blocks.definition: 80 is four twenties, with an s. From 81 on, the s goes and there is no '{et}'. 90 to 99 add 10 to 19 to four twenties. 100 is '{cent}'.

blocks.definition: French has 3 methods for asking questions. Start with the easiest!
blocks.example: 1) {Est-ce que} (easiest), 2) Intonation (informal), 3) Inversion (formal)
blocks.term: Three Ways to Ask Questions in French

blocks.definition: Add '{est-ce que}' before ANY statement to make it a question. No word order change needed!
blocks.example: Statement: '{tu as un chat}' → Question: '{est-ce que tu as un chat?}' (do you have a cat?)

blocks.definition: Put question word first, then '{est-ce que}', then statement
blocks.example: {où est-ce que tu es?} (where are you?), {quand est-ce que tu as le livre?} (when do you have the book?)

blocks.definition: Just say a statement with rising voice at the end - super informal!
blocks.example: {Tu as un chat? ↗} (you have a cat?), {Tu es où? ↗} (you are where?)

blocks.definition: Flip verb and subject, add hyphen. Used in formal/written French
blocks.example: {As-tu un chat?} (have you a cat?), {Où es-tu?} (where are you?)

blocks.definition: These words unlock every question you need: what, who, where, when, how, why, how much
blocks.example: {que}/{quoi} (what), {qui} (who), {où} (where), {quand} (when), {comment} (how), {pourquoi} (why), {combien} (how much/many)

blocks.definition: '{Que}' starts questions, '{quoi}' ends them or stands alone
blocks.example: {Que fais-tu?} (what do you do?) vs Tu fais quoi? (you do what?) vs Quoi? (what?!)

blocks.definition: Some questions are used so often they become fixed phrases
blocks.example: {qu'est-ce que c'est?} (what is it?), {comment ça va?} (how's it going?), {ça va?} (you good?), {qu'est-ce que tu veux?} (what do you want?), {est-ce que tu peux?} (can you?)

body.line: Three ways to turn any sentence into a question, and when to use each one.

parts.heading: Three ways to ask
parts.note: Start with {est-ce que}. It works for every question and changes nothing else in the sentence.
text: Every French question uses one of three methods.

build.fr: Est-ce que tu as un chat ?

blocks.heading: With a question word in front

parts.heading: {Est-ce que}
text: {Est-ce que} means roughly “is it that”. Put it in front of any statement and the statement becomes a question.

parts.heading: Raise your voice
parts.note: Same words, different tone. This is how friends talk to each other.
text: In everyday speech, French speakers often keep the statement as it is and raise their voice at the end.

parts.heading: Flip the verb
parts.note: You will see it in books, formal emails and the news.
text: For formal speech and writing, put the verb before the subject and join them with a hyphen. This is called inversion.

parts.heading: Which one to use
parts.note: Use {est-ce que} for everything at first. The other two come as you hear more French.

parts.heading: French verbs follow patterns
text: French verbs belong to groups, and verbs in a group change in similar ways. Once you hear a pattern, each new verb is easier to learn.
You learned each verb as it is written. This guide is about how the forms sound.

parts.heading: Four forms, one sound
parts.note: The spellings differ, but within each verb these four forms sound the same. That helps when you speak and when you listen.
text: Listen to {je}, {tu}, {il} and {elle} in each verb.

parts.heading: -ons for nous, -ez for vous
text: Whatever the group, {nous} and {vous} keep these endings.

parts.heading: The silent -ent
parts.note: The -ent is written but never spoken. In writing, it tells you that several people are doing something. It can change how the letters before it sound, so {ils veulent} sounds a little different from {il veut}.
text: For {ils} and {elles}, the verb ends in -ent.

parts.heading: être, avoir and aller go their own way
parts.note: Listen again: {tu} and {il} still sound the same in each of the three.
text: Some verbs are used so often that they kept forms of their own. These are the irregular verbs, and you use them so much that they stick. English does the same with am, are and is.

parts.heading: avoir and aller keep -ons and -ez
parts.note: {être} is the most used verb in French, and the most irregular.
text: Even these two keep the {nous} and {vous} endings. {être} is the one that breaks them.

parts.heading: ils and elles: {sont, ont, vont}
parts.note: In {ils ont}, the s of {ils} sounds as z before the vowel. In {ils sont}, you hear a clean s. That z is a liaison.

list: Different spellings often share one sound, so the forms you hear keep coming back.
{être}, {avoir} and {aller} are among the most irregular verbs in French, and you know them already.
Most verbs you meet next follow these patterns, starting with {partir} in the next lesson.

blocks.example: 15 total forms: MY ({mon}/{ma}/{mes}), YOUR informal ({ton}/{ta}/{tes}), HIS/HER ({son}/{sa}/{ses}), OUR ({notre}/{nos}), YOUR formal ({votre}/{vos}), THEIR ({leur}/{leurs})

blocks.definition: The possessive adjective matches the gender/number of the THING being owned, NOT the owner
blocks.example: Marie's book = {SON livre} (masculine '{son}' because '{livre}' is masculine, even though Marie is female). Pierre's house = {SA maison} (feminine '{sa}' because '{maison}' is feminine, even though Pierre is male)
blocks.term: 🔑 CRITICAL RULE: Agreement with the THING owned

blocks.definition: French has two ways to say 'your' depending on relationship and respect level
blocks.example: INFORMAL with friends/family: {ton}/{ta}/{tes} ({ton frère}, {ta sœur}, {tes amis}). FORMAL with strangers/respect: {votre}/{vos} ({votre bureau}, {vos bagages})

blocks.definition: Some possessives don't change for masculine/feminine - only for singular/plural
blocks.example: {NOTRE}/{NOS} (our): {notre maison}, {notre jardin}, {nos enfants. VOTRE}/{VOS} (your formal): {votre livre}, {votre famille}, {vos idées. LEUR}/{LEURS} (their): {leur chat}, {leur maison}, {leurs amis}

blocks.definition: Each owner has a predictable number of forms to memorize
blocks.example: MY, YOUR (informal), HIS/HER = 3 forms each (masc/fem/plural). OUR, YOUR (formal), THEIR = 2 forms each (singular/plural only)

text: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and you learn each one with {un} or {une}. Some endings go with one gender most of the time, so the ending of a new noun usually tells you its article.

parts.heading: Feminine: -tion, -té, -ure
text: Most nouns that end in -tion, -té or -ure take {une} and {la}.

parts.heading: Masculine: -ment, -age, -eau
parts.note: {l'eau} (water) ends in -eau but is feminine, and a few nouns that end in -age are feminine too. Learn each noun with its article.
text: Most nouns that end in -ment, -age or -eau take {un} and {le}.

parts.heading: Why gender helps
text: A noun's gender sets its article and the form of any adjective that goes with it.

passage.en: The city of Arles. Vincent van Gogh and Paul Gauguin meet at their favorite café to drink their favorite drink, absinthe. It is sometimes said to make one see green fairies.
passage.fr: La ville d'Arles. Vincent van Gogh et Paul Gauguin se retrouvent à leur café préféré pour boire leur boisson favorite, l'absinthe. On dit parfois qu'elle fait voir des fées vertes.

passage.en: Vincent van Gogh and Paul Gauguin are talking in a café in Arles.
passage.fr: Vincent van Gogh et Paul Gauguin parlent dans un café à Arles.

img.alt: Vincent van Gogh, in a straw hat and blue jacket, shakes hands with Paul Gauguin, in a red scarf, beside the yellow café terrace under a starry sky.

passage.en: "Hi Vincent!" says Paul.
passage.fr: « Salut Vincent ! » dit Paul.

passage.en: "Hi Paul, my friend!" says Vincent.
passage.fr: « Salut Paul, mon ami ! » dit Vincent.

passage.en: "How are you?" asks Paul.
passage.fr: « Comment ça va ? » demande Paul.

passage.en: "Good, and you?"
passage.fr: « Bien, et toi ? »

passage.en: "Very good, thanks. We ate here yesterday," says Paul.
passage.fr: « Très bien, merci. Nous avons mangé ici hier, » dit Paul.

passage.en: "Yes. It was good," says Vincent.
passage.fr: « Oui. C'était bon, » dit Vincent.

passage.en: "What do you want to drink?" Paul asks.
passage.fr: « Qu'est-ce que tu veux boire ? » demande Paul.

passage.en: "I want an absinthe, what else?" says Vincent.
passage.fr: « Je veux une absinthe, quoi d'autre ? » dit Vincent.

passage.en: "Me too. I like absinthe," says Paul.
passage.fr: « Moi aussi. J'aime l'absinthe, » dit Paul.

passage.en: The waiter brings their absinthes. They drink a lot. They like it.
passage.fr: Le serveur apporte leurs absinthes. Ils boivent beaucoup. Ils l'aiment.

img.alt: A waiter pours water as Vincent and Paul raise two glasses of pale green absinthe at their table on the terrace.

passage.en: Vincent looks around the café.
passage.fr: Vincent regarde autour du café.

passage.en: "This café is very beautiful," he says. "I want to do something."
passage.fr: « Ce café est très beau, » il dit. « Je veux faire quelque chose. »

passage.en: "What do you want to do?" asks Paul.
passage.fr: « Qu'est-ce que tu veux faire ? » demande Paul.

passage.en: "I want to make a painting of this café at night."
passage.fr: « Je veux faire un tableau de ce café la nuit. »

passage.en: "Good idea!" says Paul. "This café is more beautiful at night than during the day, isn't it?"
passage.fr: « Bonne idée ! » dit Paul. « Ce café est plus beau la nuit que le jour, n'est-ce pas ? »

passage.en: Vincent says, "Yes! The colors are better in the evening. And the stars are beautiful."
passage.fr: Vincent dit : « Oui ! Les couleurs sont meilleures le soir. Et les étoiles sont belles. »

passage.en: "Excuse me," says Vincent. "I'm going to my hotel. I'm going to look for my paints."
passage.fr: « Excusez-moi, » dit Vincent. « Je vais à mon hôtel. Je vais chercher mes peintures. »

passage.en: "Right now?" asks Paul.
passage.fr: « Maintenant ? » demande Paul.

passage.en: "Yes... this evening..." says Vincent.
passage.fr: « Oui... ce soir... » dit Vincent.

passage.en: "Ah, I love it!" says Paul.
passage.fr: « Ah, j'adore ça ! » dit Paul.

passage.en: Vincent leaves for his hotel. He finds his paints. He returns to the café.
passage.fr: Vincent part pour son hôtel. Il trouve ses peintures. Il revient au café.

img.alt: Vincent hurries down a cobbled street at night with his paint box and easel under his arm, the lit café at the end of the street.

passage.en: Two hours later
passage.fr: Deux heures plus tard

passage.en: Vincent makes his painting. Paul drinks his absinthe.
passage.fr: Vincent fait son tableau. Paul boit son absinthe.

passage.en: "How do you do that?" asks Paul. "You see the colors at night?"
passage.fr: « Comment tu fais ça ? » demande Paul. « Tu vois les couleurs la nuit ? »

passage.en: "Yes, I see everything," says Vincent. "I see the café, I see the stars, I see the people."
passage.fr: « Oui, je vois tout, » dit Vincent. « Je vois le café, je vois les étoiles, je vois les gens. »

passage.en: They drink more absinthe.
passage.fr: Ils boivent encore de l'absinthe.

img.alt: Vincent paints the café terrace at his easel while Paul watches from the table with a glass of absinthe.

passage.en: Paul says, "You are a great artist, Vincent."
passage.fr: Paul dit : « Tu es un grand artiste, Vincent. »

passage.en: "Thank you, my friend," says Vincent. "I love Arles. Arles is beautiful. This café is my favorite café."
passage.fr: « Merci, mon ami, » dit Vincent. « J'aime Arles. Arles est belle. Ce café est mon café préféré. »

passage.en: They drink a lot of their absinthes. Vincent continues his painting (tableau) of the café at night.
passage.fr: Ils boivent beaucoup de leurs absinthes. Vincent continue son tableau du café la nuit.

passage.en: Paul says, "This painting (tableau) is better than your other paintings (tableaux)."
passage.fr: Paul dit : « Ce tableau est meilleur que tes autres tableaux. »

passage.en: Vincent smiles. "Maybe. We'll see."
passage.fr: Vincent sourit. « Peut-être. Nous allons voir. »

passage.en: They are at the café all night. Vincent makes his painting (tableau). Paul drinks his absinthe with him.
passage.fr: Ils sont au café toute la nuit. Vincent fait son tableau. Paul boit son absinthe avec lui.

img.alt: Seen from behind, Vincent and Paul sit on a bench on the empty terrace, looking at the finished painting on its easel as the sky starts to lighten.

passage.en: It's a good night in Arles.
passage.fr: C'est une bonne nuit à Arles.

passage.en: "I call it: Café Terrace at Night," says Vincent.
passage.fr: « Je l'appelle : Terrasse du café le soir, » dit Vincent.

passage.en: The End.
passage.fr: Fin.

parts.heading: One stem, two endings

text: The future and the conditional are built on the same stem, and only the ending changes. The stem of {faire} is fer-. The future adds -ai for {je}, and the conditional adds -ais.

parts.heading: {faire} and {aller} in both tenses
text: Side by side, the future and the conditional of a verb keep one stem. For an -er verb such as {parler}, the stem is the whole infinitive: {je parlerai}. {aller} has a short stem of its own, ir-.

passage.en: What is learning? Actually, it's a big question. Everyone studies, but does everyone learn well?
passage.fr: Qu'est-ce que l'apprentissage? En fait, c'est une grande question. Tout le monde étudie, mais est-ce que tout le monde apprend bien?

passage.en: A student thinks about a big question.
passage.fr: Une étudiante pense à une grande question.

img.alt: A young woman in a white dress and red shawl sits at a candlelit desk of open books and scrolls, chin on her hand, deep in thought.

passage.en: Well, I think that learning goes with a question. When we have a question, we want to study. We look for an answer. So, questions are very good for learning.
passage.fr: Bon, je pense que l'apprentissage va avec une question. Quand on a une question, on veut étudier. On cherche une réponse. Donc, les questions sont très bonnes pour apprendre.

passage.en: But studying isn't the same thing as learning. I can study for hours, but if I don't understand, I'm not really learning. Learning is when I understand an idea.
passage.fr: Mais étudier, ce n'est pas la même chose qu'apprendre. Je peux étudier pendant des heures, mais si je ne comprends pas, je n'apprends pas vraiment. L'apprentissage, c'est quand je comprends une idée.

passage.en: So, how do we learn well? Here are my thoughts:
passage.fr: Alors, comment est-ce qu'on apprend bien? Voici mes pensées:

passage.en: First, we must ask questions. Socrates thinks that questions are essential. If we don't ask questions, we don't think. And if we don't think, we don't understand.
passage.fr: D'abord, on doit demander des questions. Socrate pense que les questions sont essentielles. Si on ne demande pas de questions, on ne pense pas. Et si on ne pense pas, on ne comprend pas.

passage.en: Socrates asks his students questions.
passage.fr: Socrate demande des questions à ses étudiants.

img.alt: Socrates, white-bearded, raises a finger as he questions a group of young students under a stone colonnade.

passage.en: Next, we must study well. We can't learn if we study poorly. Study requires time.
passage.fr: Ensuite, on doit étudier bien. On ne peut pas apprendre si on étudie mal. L'étude demande du temps.

passage.en: After that, we must review. Review is very good. When we review, we understand better. We see the things between ideas.
passage.fr: Après, on doit réviser. La révision est très bonne. Quand on révise, on comprend mieux. On voit les choses entre les idées.

passage.en: She reviews. She sees the things between ideas.
passage.fr: Elle révise. Elle voit les choses entre les idées.

img.alt: The student reviews loose pages of notes spread across her table by candlelight, a bust of a philosopher behind her.

passage.en: Finally, we must believe in ourselves. If we don't believe we can learn, we're not going to learn.
passage.fr: Finalement, on doit croire en soi. Si on ne croit pas qu'on peut apprendre, on ne va pas apprendre.

passage.en: I know many students. Some think they're not good at learning. But actually, everyone can learn. It's a question of method.
passage.fr: Je connais beaucoup d'étudiants. Certains pensent qu'ils ne sont pas bons en apprentissage. Mais en fait, tout le monde peut apprendre. C'est une question de méthode.

passage.en: Even things are better with time. Now, I understand a lot. I know how to speak a little. I know words, phrases, ideas.
passage.fr: Même les choses sont meilleures avec le temps. Maintenant, je comprends beaucoup. Je sais parler un peu. Je connais des mots, des phrases, des idées.

passage.en: So, learning is a journey. We want an answer. We study. We search. We find answers. We understand. And finally, we know. It's magnificent, you know!
passage.fr: Donc, l'apprentissage est un voyage. On veut une réponse. On étudie. On cherche. On trouve des réponses. On comprend. Et finalement, on sait. C'est magnifique, quoi!

passage.en: Learning is a journey.
passage.fr: L'apprentissage est un voyage.

img.alt: The student walks a dirt road at sunrise with a book under her arm, a small Greek temple on a hill in the distance.

passage.en: Actually, you're learning right now. You understand my ideas. That's proof that you can learn. You're already doing it!
passage.fr: En fait, vous êtes en train d'apprendre maintenant. Vous comprenez mes idées. C'est la preuve que vous pouvez apprendre. Vous le faites déjà!

passage.en: My name is Marie. Here is my typical day.
passage.fr: Je m'appelle Marie. Voici ma journée typique.

passage.en: First, I wake up at seven o'clock. I don't get up right away. I think about my day for a few minutes.
passage.fr: D'abord, je me réveille à sept heures. Je ne me lève pas tout de suite. Je pense à ma journée pendant quelques minutes.

passage.en: Seven o’clock. Marie thinks about her day.
passage.fr: Sept heures. Marie pense à sa journée.

img.alt: Marie lies in bed in striped pyjamas, hands behind her head, her yellow sweater on a chair and Paris rooftops outside the window.

passage.en: Then, I get up. I go to the kitchen. I have my coffee. Before coffee, I can't think well!
passage.fr: Ensuite, je me lève. Je vais dans la cuisine. Je prends mon café. Avant le café, je ne peux pas penser bien!

passage.en: Marie has her coffee.
passage.fr: Marie prend son café.

img.alt: Marie, in striped pyjamas, holds a big steaming bowl of coffee in her bright kitchen.

passage.en: After coffee, I wash and get dressed. I get ready for the Sorbonne. I must hurry because my class is at nine o'clock.
passage.fr: Après le café, je me lave et je m'habille. Je me prépare pour la Sorbonne. Je dois me dépêcher parce que mon cours est à neuf heures.

passage.en: At the Sorbonne, I study French. I like my classes. I understand well now. Before, I didn't understand everything, but now, I know many things. My teacher tells me: "Listen well! Think in French! Speak with your friends!"
passage.fr: À la Sorbonne, j'étudie le français. J'aime mes cours. Je comprends bien maintenant. Avant, je ne comprenais pas tout, mais maintenant, je sais beaucoup de choses. Mon professeur me dit: "Écoute bien! Pense en français! Parle avec tes amis!"

passage.en: During class, we learn new words. We ask ourselves questions. We have fun too. The students help each other. We understand each other well.
passage.fr: Pendant le cours, on apprend des mots nouveaux. On se pose des questions. On s'amuse aussi. Les étudiants s'aident. Nous nous comprenons bien.

passage.en: At the Sorbonne, the students help each other.
passage.fr: À la Sorbonne, les étudiants s’aident.

img.alt: Marie raises her hand, smiling, among laughing classmates while the teacher talks at the blackboard.

passage.en: After classes, I review my lessons. I remember everything that we learn. Then, I go eat with my friends. We see each other often. We speak to each other in French. It's magnificent, you know!
passage.fr: Après les cours, je révise mes leçons. Je me souviens de tout ce qu'on apprend. Puis, je vais manger avec mes amis. On se voit souvent. On se parle en français. C'est magnifique, quoi!

passage.en: Marie eats with her friends. They speak French to each other.
passage.fr: Marie mange avec ses amis. Ils se parlent en français.

img.alt: Marie laughs with three friends over lunch at a café terrace under a red and yellow awning.

passage.en: Finally, I return home. I'm happy. I think: "Today, I learned well. Tomorrow, I'm going to learn even more."
passage.fr: Finalement, je rentre chez moi. Je suis contente. Je pense: "Aujourd'hui, j'ai bien appris. Demain, je vais apprendre encore plus."

passage.en: In the evening, Marie goes home.
passage.fr: Le soir, Marie rentre chez elle.

img.alt: Marie walks home along the Seine with her bag over her shoulder, Notre-Dame across the river.

blocks.definition: PASSÉ COMPOSÉ = Specific completed action (What happened?). IMPARFAIT = Ongoing state/description/habit (How things were/used to be)

blocks.definition: Combine: 1) Scene-setting (IMP), 2) Events (PC), 3) Causal reasoning (parce que, car), 4) Spatial context (près de, devant)

passage.en: Yesterday, it was Saturday and the weather was very nice in Paris. I was happy because it was the weekend and I had no work.
passage.fr: Hier, c'était samedi et il faisait très beau à Paris. J'étais content parce que c'était le week-end et je n'avais pas de travail.

passage.en: First, I woke up at 8am. Usually, I used to get up later on Saturdays, but that day, I wanted to go out early because the weather was so nice.
passage.fr: D'abord, je me suis réveillé à 8h. D'habitude, je me levais plus tard le samedi, mais ce jour-là, j'ai voulu sortir tôt parce que le temps était si beau.

passage.en: After my coffee, I went to Jardin du Luxembourg near my house. I really like this park! There were many people in the garden. It was a beautiful day.
passage.fr: Après mon café, je suis allé au Jardin du Luxembourg près de ma maison. J'aime beaucoup ce parc! Il y avait beaucoup de gens dans le jardin. C'était une belle journée.

passage.en: A Saturday morning in the Jardin du Luxembourg.
passage.fr: Un samedi matin au Jardin du Luxembourg.

img.alt: Impressionist painting of a young man in a straw hat and cream jacket walking toward the pond of the Jardin du Luxembourg, with toy sailboats, strollers and the Luxembourg Palace behind.

passage.en: I went near the lake when suddenly I saw my friend Pierre. He was sitting on a bench under a big tree. I went towards him and we started talking.
passage.fr: Je suis allé près du lac quand soudain j'ai vu mon ami Pierre. Il était assis sur un banc sous un grand arbre. Je suis allé vers lui et on a commencé à parler.

passage.en: Pierre is sitting on a bench under a big tree.
passage.fr: Pierre est assis sur un banc, sous un grand arbre.

img.alt: Impressionist painting of Pierre, bearded in a bowler hat, waving from a green bench under a big tree beside the pond as the narrator walks up.

passage.en: "Hi Pierre! What are you doing here?" I asked.
passage.fr: "Salut Pierre! Qu'est-ce que tu fais ici?" j'ai demandé.

passage.en: "Hello! I wanted to be outside because it was so nice. I'm glad you're here!" he said.
passage.fr: "Bonjour! Je voulais être dehors parce qu'il faisait si beau. Je suis content que tu sois là!" il a dit.

passage.en: We talked for an hour. He told me he wanted a new job at the Sorbonne because he didn't like his job. I told him that I understood because I had the same problem last year.
passage.fr: Nous avons parlé pendant une heure. Il m'a dit qu'il voulait un nouveau travail à la Sorbonne parce qu'il n'aimait pas son travail. Je lui ai dit que je comprenais car j'ai eu le même problème l'année dernière.

passage.en: Then, since we were hungry, we decided to go to Café de Flore which is across from the garden. Café de Flore is very good and very famous in Paris! There were many people - next to the windows, around the tables, everywhere!
passage.fr: Ensuite, comme nous avions faim, nous avons décidé d'aller au Café de Flore qui est en face du jardin. Le Café de Flore est très bon et très célèbre à Paris! Il y avait beaucoup de gens - à côté des fenêtres, autour des tables, partout!

passage.en: We ordered sandwiches and coffee. While we were eating, we saw Marie. She entered the café. She saw us and she came to our table.
passage.fr: Nous avons commandé des sandwichs et du café. Pendant que nous mangions, nous avons vu Marie. Elle est entrée dans le café. Elle nous a vus et elle est venue à notre table.

passage.en: At Café de Flore, Marie comes to our table.
passage.fr: Au Café de Flore, Marie vient à notre table.

img.alt: Impressionist painting of a crowded Paris café with red banquettes and mirrors; the narrator and Pierre look up from their coffee as Marie, in a lavender dress, arrives at their table.

passage.en: "What a surprise!" she said. "I didn't know you were here!"
passage.fr: "Quelle surprise!" elle a dit. "Je ne savais pas que vous étiez ici!"

passage.en: Marie was our friend from the Sorbonne. We haven't seen her for six months because she's now in Lyon. Thanks to this meeting, we were able to be together for the afternoon.
passage.fr: Marie était notre amie de la Sorbonne. Nous ne l'avons pas vue depuis six mois parce qu'elle est maintenant à Lyon. Grâce à cette rencontre, nous avons pu être ensemble pour l'après-midi.

passage.en: In the afternoon, we went to the cinema near the station. There was the film "Amélie" - a very good French film! The cinema was ten minutes from Café de Flore.
passage.fr: L'après-midi, nous sommes allés au cinéma près de la gare. Il y avait le film "Amélie" - un très bon film français! Le cinéma était à dix minutes du Café de Flore.

passage.en: The film was excellent! We really liked Amélie. After the film, we decided to eat together at Restaurant Le Procope which is behind the cinema. Le Procope is the oldest restaurant in Paris!
passage.fr: Le film était excellent! Nous avons beaucoup aimé Amélie. Après le film, nous avons décidé de manger ensemble au Restaurant Le Procope qui est derrière le cinéma. Le Procope est le plus vieux restaurant de Paris!

passage.en: At the restaurant, we ate good French food. It was delicious! We talked about the Sorbonne, about our lives, and about what we want to do.
passage.fr: Au restaurant, nous avons mangé de la bonne cuisine française. C'était délicieux! Nous avons parlé de la Sorbonne, de nos vies, et de ce que nous voulons faire.

passage.en: In the evening at Le Procope, the oldest restaurant in Paris.
passage.fr: Le soir, au Procope, le plus vieux restaurant de Paris.

img.alt: Impressionist painting of the three friends laughing at a round table in a red restaurant with chandeliers and gilt frames.

passage.en: Because of the time, Marie had to leave around 9pm to go back to Lyon. Pierre and I stayed a bit longer. We had one last coffee together.
passage.fr: À cause du temps, Marie a dû partir vers 9h pour rentrer à Lyon. Pierre et moi sommes restés un peu plus. Nous avons pris un dernier café ensemble.

passage.en: Finally, I went home around 10pm. I was tired but very happy. It was a perfect day in Paris.
passage.fr: Finalement, je suis rentré chez moi vers 10h. J'étais fatigué mais très heureux. C'était une journée parfaite à Paris.

passage.en: Around 10pm, I walk home, tired but happy.
passage.fr: Vers 10h, je rentre chez moi, fatigué mais heureux.

img.alt: Impressionist painting of the narrator walking home alone at night along a tree-lined Paris street lit by gas lamps, smiling.

passage.en: Sometimes, the best days are the ones we don't think we'll have. Thanks to my outing to Jardin du Luxembourg, I had a very beautiful day with my friends.
passage.fr: Parfois, les meilleures journées sont celles qu'on ne pense pas avoir. Grâce à ma sortie au Jardin du Luxembourg, j'ai eu une très belle journée avec mes amis.

passage.en: Before sleeping, I thought: "That's why I love Saturdays in Paris!"
passage.fr: Avant de dormir, j'ai pensé: "C'est pour ça que j'aime les samedis à Paris!"

passage.en: The End
passage.fr: Fin

blocks.definition: French uses different verb forms after phrases like '{il faut que}' (someone needs to), '{je veux que}' (I want someone to), '{je suis content que}' (I'm happy that someone...). These express wishes, needs, or emotions about OTHER PEOPLE's actions.
blocks.example: Normal statement: {Tu es sage} (You are good). Wish about you: {Il faut que tu sois sage} (You need to be good - different form!)

blocks.definition: ONLY after certain phrases: il faut que, je veux que, je suis content que, j'ai peur que, avant que, pour que, bien que, etc.
blocks.example: ✓ {Il faut que tu sois sage} (You need to be good), ✓ {Je veux qu'il aille} (I want him to go)
blocks.term: Where You CAN Use These Forms

blocks.definition: DON'T use these for normal statements, questions, or with just il faut/je veux (no '{que}')
blocks.example: ✗ {Tu sois content?} (Wrong! Say: {Tu es content?}). ✗ {Il faut aller} (Correct - no '{que}' = normal form)
blocks.term: Where You CANNOT Use These Forms

blocks.definition: If you see '{que}' + a person after these starter phrases, use these forms!
blocks.example: {il faut QUE tu} → use sois/{aies}/{ailles}/{fasses, je veux QUE tu} → use sois/aies/ailles/{fasses}

passage.en: My name is Sophie and I've been living in Paris for five years. I love this city! But I always have a big dream: I want my life to be different.
passage.fr: Je m'appelle Sophie et j'habite à Paris depuis cinq ans. J'adore cette ville! Mais j'ai toujours un grand rêve: je veux que ma vie soit différente.

passage.en: Last night, I was sitting in a small café near Notre-Dame. I was looking at the beautiful cathedral and thinking about my dreams. It was cold but I was happy to be there.
passage.fr: Hier soir, j'étais assise dans un petit café près de Notre-Dame. Je regardais la belle cathédrale et je pensais à mes rêves. Il faisait froid mais j'étais contente d'être là.

passage.en: Sophie looks at Notre-Dame and thinks about her dreams.
passage.fr: Sophie regarde Notre-Dame et pense à ses rêves.

img.alt: Chagall-style painting of Sophie, in a red coat and yellow scarf, holding a coffee at a small café table and gazing at Notre-Dame in the blue dusk.

passage.en: I had already finished my work for the day. I had already thought about many things. Now, I just wanted to dream a little.
passage.fr: J'avais déjà fini mon travail pour la journée. J'avais déjà pensé à beaucoup de choses. Maintenant, je voulais simplement rêver un peu.

passage.en: If I were rich, I'd buy a small house in Montmartre. I'd like to live in this famous neighborhood where artists have lived. If I had more money, I'd also travel to Nice and Bordeaux.
passage.fr: Si j'étais riche, j'achèterais une petite maison à Montmartre. J'aimerais habiter dans ce quartier célèbre où les artistes ont vécu. Si j'avais plus d'argent, je voyagerais aussi à Nice et à Bordeaux.

passage.en: Sophie's dream: a small house in Montmartre.
passage.fr: Le rêve de Sophie : une petite maison à Montmartre.

img.alt: Chagall-style painting of Sophie floating over the rooftops of Montmartre, past a windmill and the white domes of Sacré-Cœur, toward a small house with a red door.

passage.en: My friend Marc arrived at the café. He knew I like this café because it's near Notre-Dame. I'm glad he came! We always talk to each other about our dreams.
passage.fr: Mon ami Marc est arrivé au café. Il savait que j'aime ce café parce que c'est près de Notre-Dame. Je suis contente qu'il soit venu! On se parle toujours de nos rêves.

passage.en: "Hi Sophie! I knew you'd be here," he said.
passage.fr: "Salut Sophie! Je savais que tu serais ici," il a dit.

passage.en: "Hello Marc! I'm happy you're here. I was thinking about my dreams," I said.
passage.fr: "Bonjour Marc! Je suis heureuse que tu sois là. J'étais en train de penser à mes rêves," j'ai dit.

passage.en: "Oh yes? Me too, I have many dreams. I want my life to change," he said.
passage.fr: "Ah oui? Moi aussi, j'ai beaucoup de rêves. Je veux que ma vie change," il a dit.

passage.en: Marc told me he wanted to be an artist. He wanted people to see his paintings at the Louvre one day. It's a big dream! The Louvre is the most famous museum in the world.
passage.fr: Marc m'a dit qu'il voulait être artiste. Il voulait que les gens voient ses peintures au Louvre un jour. C'est un grand rêve! Le Louvre est le musée le plus célèbre du monde.

passage.en: "I want my paintings to be at the Louvre one day. But I'm afraid it might be difficult," he said.
passage.fr: "Je veux qu'un jour mes peintures soient au Louvre. Mais j'ai peur que ce soit difficile," il a dit.

passage.en: Marc's dream: his paintings in the Louvre.
passage.fr: Le rêve de Marc : ses peintures au Louvre.

img.alt: Chagall-style painting of Marc, in a paint-stained green jacket, flying with his brush and palette as his canvases drift toward the Louvre pyramid.

passage.en: "I understand. But you have to try! If you don't do anything, you'll never know," I said.
passage.fr: "Je comprends. Mais il faut que tu essaies! Si tu ne fais rien, tu ne sauras jamais," j'ai dit.

passage.en: We talked for an hour. I told him I wanted to be a French teacher. I'd like my students to love the French language like me.
passage.fr: Nous avons parlé pendant une heure. Je lui ai dit que je voulais être professeur de français. J'aimerais que mes étudiants adorent la langue française comme moi.

passage.en: "I'm glad you have this dream. You'd be an excellent teacher," Marc said.
passage.fr: "Je suis content que tu aies ce rêve. Tu serais une excellente professeur," Marc a dit.

passage.en: "Thank you! But I'm afraid it might be too difficult. I had already tried last year but I didn't succeed," I said.
passage.fr: "Merci! Mais j'ai peur que ce soit trop difficile. J'avais déjà essayé l'année dernière mais je n'ai pas réussi," j'ai dit.

passage.en: "You have to try again! If I were you, I wouldn't give up," he said.
passage.fr: "Il faut que tu essaies encore! Si j'étais toi, je ne renoncerais pas," il a dit.

passage.en: Marc was right. Before we talked, I had already lost hope. But now, I feel better.
passage.fr: Marc avait raison. Avant que nous parlions, j'avais déjà perdu espoir. Mais maintenant, je me sens mieux.

passage.en: We decided to help each other. I want him to succeed with his paintings, and he wants me to succeed as a teacher.
passage.fr: Nous avons décidé d'aider l'un l'autre. Je veux qu'il réussisse avec ses peintures, et il veut que je réussisse comme professeur.

passage.en: "I'm happy we're friends. We can help each other," Marc said.
passage.fr: "Je suis heureux que nous soyons amis. On peut s'aider," Marc a dit.

passage.en: "Me too! I'd like us both to succeed," I said.
passage.fr: "Moi aussi! J'aimerais que nous réussissions tous les deux," j'ai dit.

passage.en: After our coffee, we walked towards the Seine. It was night now and Paris was magnificent. The lights of the Eiffel Tower were shining in the distance.
passage.fr: Après notre café, nous avons marché vers la Seine. Il faisait nuit maintenant et Paris était magnifique. Les lumières de la Tour Eiffel brillaient au loin.

passage.en: Sophie and Marc walk toward the Seine.
passage.fr: Sophie et Marc marchent vers la Seine.

img.alt: Chagall-style painting of Sophie and Marc walking along the Seine at night toward a stone bridge, the Eiffel Tower glowing gold in the distance.

passage.en: "If we had more time, we could walk all night," Marc said.
passage.fr: "Si on avait plus de temps, on pourrait marcher toute la nuit," Marc a dit.

passage.en: "Yes! I love Paris at night. That's why I want to stay here all my life," I said.
passage.fr: "Oui ! J'adore Paris la nuit. C'est pour ça que je veux rester ici toute ma vie," j'ai dit.

passage.en: We said goodbye near the bridge. Before leaving, Marc told me something important.
passage.fr: Nous nous sommes dit au revoir près du pont. Avant de partir, Marc m'a dit quelque chose d'important.

passage.en: "Sophie, you need to know one thing: your dreams are important. I want you to keep trying," he said.
passage.fr: "Sophie, il faut que tu saches une chose: tes rêves sont importants. Je veux que tu continues à essayer," il a dit.

passage.en: "Thank you Marc. I'm grateful you told me that. You too, you must continue with your paintings," I said.
passage.fr: "Merci Marc. Je suis reconnaissante que tu m'aies dit ça. Toi aussi, tu dois continuer avec tes peintures," j'ai dit.

passage.en: Walking home, I thought about our conversation. I regret that I lost hope before. But now, I'm glad Marc is my friend.
passage.fr: En rentrant chez moi, j'ai pensé à notre conversation. Je regrette que j'aie perdu espoir avant. Mais maintenant, je suis contente que Marc soit mon ami.

passage.en: If I had known earlier that hope was so important, I would have continued my studies. But it's not too late!
passage.fr: Si j'avais su plus tôt que l'espoir était si important, j'aurais continué mes études. Mais il n'est pas trop tard!

passage.en: Tomorrow, I'm going to call the university. I need to ask for information to become a teacher. I want my dreams to become reality.
passage.fr: Demain, je vais appeler l'université. Il faut que je demande des informations pour devenir professeur. Je veux que mes rêves deviennent réalité.

passage.en: A new day for Sophie.
passage.fr: Un nouveau jour pour Sophie.

img.alt: Chagall-style painting of Sophie at the open window of her apartment at sunrise, arms open, above the rooftops of Paris.

passage.en: Thanks to my friend and to this beautiful evening in Paris, I found my courage again. I'm happy this city exists, and I'm glad my friends support me.
passage.fr: Grâce à mon ami et à cette belle soirée à Paris, j'ai retrouvé mon courage. Je suis heureuse que cette ville existe, et je suis contente que mes amis me soutiennent.

passage.en: Like Marc said: you have to try! If we don't do anything, we'll never know. And me, I want to know if my dreams can become reality.
passage.fr: Comme Marc a dit: il faut essayer! Si on ne fait rien, on ne saura jamais. Et moi, je veux savoir si mes rêves peuvent devenir réalité.

passage.en: The End
passage.fr: Fin

passage.en: My name is Sophie and I've been living in Paris for five years. I love this city! But I always have a big dream: I want my life to be different.
passage.fr: Je m'appelle Sophie et j'habite à Paris depuis cinq ans. J'adore cette ville! Mais j'ai toujours un grand rêve: je veux que ma vie soit différente.

passage.en: Last night, I was sitting in a small café near Notre-Dame. I was looking at the beautiful cathedral and thinking about my dreams. It was cold but I was happy to be there.
passage.fr: Hier soir, j'étais assise dans un petit café près de Notre-Dame. Je regardais la belle cathédrale et je pensais à mes rêves. Il faisait froid mais j'étais contente d'être là.

passage.en: Sophie looks at Notre-Dame and thinks about her dreams.
passage.fr: Sophie regarde Notre-Dame et pense à ses rêves.

img.alt: Chagall-style painting of Sophie, in a red coat and yellow scarf, holding a coffee at a small café table and gazing at Notre-Dame in the blue dusk.

passage.en: Modern France is a country that continues to evolve rapidly. With its sixty-eight million inhabitants, it remains an important nation in Europe and in the world.
passage.fr: La France d'aujourd'hui est un pays qui continue à évoluer rapidement. Avec ses soixante-huit millions d'habitants, elle reste une nation importante en Europe et dans le monde.

passage.en: Paris, its capital, has more than two million people. This magnificent city attracts millions of visitors each year. They come to admire its famous monuments like the Eiffel Tower, Notre-Dame, the Louvre, and the Arc de Triomphe on the Champs-Élysées. Many also visit the Palace of Versailles. Tourists often look for directions to find these historic places.
passage.fr: Paris, sa capitale, compte plus de deux millions de personnes. Cette ville magnifique attire des millions de visiteurs chaque année. Ils viennent admirer ses monuments célèbres comme la Tour Eiffel, Notre-Dame, le Louvre, et l'Arc de Triomphe sur les Champs-Élysées. Beaucoup visitent aussi le château de Versailles. Les touristes cherchent souvent des directions pour trouver ces lieux historiques.

passage.en: The Eiffel Tower, the Arc de Triomphe, the Louvre and Notre-Dame.
passage.fr: La Tour Eiffel, l'Arc de Triomphe, le Louvre et Notre-Dame.

img.alt: Art Deco poster of Paris at dusk in navy, cream and red: the Eiffel Tower in steep perspective, crowds walking up the Champs-Élysées to the Arc de Triomphe, the Louvre pyramid and Notre-Dame.

passage.en: The French educational system is internationally recognized. French students work hard in their schools and universities. They study many different subjects: sciences, history, foreign languages, and literature. Learning begins very young - children are generally six years old when they arrive at elementary school.
passage.fr: Le système éducatif français est reconnu internationalement. Les étudiants français travaillent dur dans leurs écoles et universités. Ils étudient beaucoup de matières différentes : les sciences, l'histoire, les langues étrangères, et la littérature. L'apprentissage commence très jeune - les enfants ont généralement six ans quand ils arrivent à l'école primaire.

passage.en: At six, children start elementary school.
passage.fr: À six ans, les enfants arrivent à l'école primaire.

img.alt: Art Deco poster of a classroom: young children raise their hands while a teacher points at shapes on the blackboard, beside a globe and stacked books.

passage.en: French culture influences the entire world. French artists like Claude Monet, Auguste Renoir, and Vincent van Gogh created magnificent works. These Impressionist painters still live in collective memory. Today, new artists often live in neighborhoods like Montmartre, near the famous Moulin Rouge.
passage.fr: La culture française influence le monde entier. Les artistes français comme Claude Monet, Auguste Renoir, et Vincent van Gogh ont créé des œuvres magnifiques. Ces peintres impressionnistes vivent encore dans la mémoire collective. Aujourd'hui, les nouveaux artistes vivent souvent dans des quartiers comme Montmartre, près du célèbre Moulin Rouge.

passage.en: French cuisine also remains very popular worldwide. Traditional dishes like coq au vin, ratatouille, and Marseille's bouillabaisse give pleasure to millions of people. French restaurants create unforgettable culinary experiences.
passage.fr: La cuisine française reste également très populaire dans le monde. Les plats traditionnels comme le coq au vin, la ratatouille, et la bouillabaisse de Marseille donnent du plaisir à des millions de personnes. Les restaurants français créent des expériences culinaires inoubliables.

passage.en: The French economy depends on several important sectors. Many French people work in services, others in industry or agriculture. French companies export their products to the east, west, north and south - throughout Europe and beyond.
passage.fr: L'économie française dépend de plusieurs secteurs importants. Beaucoup de Français travaillent dans les services, d'autres dans l'industrie ou l'agriculture. Les entreprises françaises exportent leurs produits vers l'est, l'ouest, le nord et le sud - dans toute l'Europe et au-delà.

passage.en: Public transportation works very well in France. Fast trains connect major cities like Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, and Nice. Travelers can arrive quickly at their destination. In Paris, the metro allows inhabitants to move around easily. They wait only a few minutes between trains.
passage.fr: Le transport public fonctionne très bien en France. Les trains rapides connectent les grandes villes comme Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, et Nice. Les voyageurs peuvent arriver rapidement à leur destination. Dans Paris, le métro permet aux habitants de se déplacer facilement. Ils attendent quelques minutes seulement entre les trains.

passage.en: A fast train crosses the countryside toward the south.
passage.fr: Un train rapide traverse la campagne vers le sud.

img.alt: Art Deco poster of a high-speed train racing across a stone viaduct over vineyards, with a metro train leaving a tunnel and travellers pulling suitcases below.

passage.en: The French love their vacations. In summer, they often travel south to enjoy the sun and the Mediterranean Sea. Nice and Cannes are very popular destinations. Others prefer to stay in their region and discover the beauty of the French countryside.
passage.fr: Les Français adorent leurs vacances. En été, ils voyagent souvent vers le sud pour profiter du soleil et de la mer Méditerranée. Nice et Cannes sont des destinations très populaires. D'autres préfèrent rester dans leur région et découvrir la beauté de la campagne française.

passage.en: Summer in Nice, on the Mediterranean.
passage.fr: L'été à Nice, au bord de la Méditerranée.

img.alt: Art Deco poster of Nice in summer: palm trees along the curving seafront promenade, blue parasols on the beach, swimmers and a sailboat under a huge golden sun.

passage.en: Technology is also changing daily life in France. Young French people listen to music online, watch movies on the internet, and communicate with their friends via their phones. This generation lives differently from their parents, but keeps important French values.
passage.fr: La technologie change aussi la vie quotidienne en France. Les jeunes Français écoutent de la musique en ligne, regardent des films sur internet, et communiquent avec leurs amis via leurs téléphones. Cette génération vit différemment de leurs parents, mais elle garde les valeurs françaises importantes.

passage.en: Today, France works actively to protect the environment. The government encourages citizens to use public transport, to recycle their waste, and to save energy. These efforts show that France thinks about the future of the planet.
passage.fr: Aujourd'hui, la France travaille activement pour protéger l'environnement. Le gouvernement encourage les citoyens à utiliser les transports publics, à recycler leurs déchets, et à économiser l'énergie. Ces efforts montrent que la France pense à l'avenir de la planète.

passage.en: By bike and by tram, France thinks about the future.
passage.fr: À vélo et en tram, la France pense à l'avenir.

img.alt: Art Deco poster of young people cycling on a green bike lane past Haussmann buildings with solar panels, a tram, recycling bins, a Gothic spire, a glass tower and wind turbines.

passage.en: International relations remain very important for France. It participates actively in European and global organizations. French diplomats travel regularly to meet their foreign counterparts. They discuss economic, political, and cultural questions.
passage.fr: Les relations internationales restent très importantes pour la France. Elle participe activement aux organisations européennes et mondiales. Les diplomates français voyagent régulièrement pour rencontrer leurs homologues étrangers. Ils discutent de questions économiques, politiques, et culturelles.

passage.en: In conclusion, modern France combines tradition and innovation. It preserves its historic heritage while embracing the changes of the twenty-first century. This nation continues to play a significant role on the international stage, and its contributions enrich our world.
passage.fr: En conclusion, la France moderne combine tradition et innovation. Elle préserve son patrimoine historique tout en embrassant les changements du vingt et unième siècle. Cette nation continue à jouer un rôle significatif sur la scène internationale, et ses contributions enrichissent notre monde.

passage.en: The End
passage.fr: Fin

blocks.heading: The French Alphabet
text: French uses the same 26 letters as English, but pronunciation is very different!

A ({ah}), B (bay), C (say), D (day), E (euh), F (eff), G (zhay), H (ash), I (ee), J (zhee), K (kah), L (ell), M (emm), N (enn), O ({oh}), P (pay), Q (koo), R ({air}), S (ess), T (tay), U (oo), V (vay), W (doo-bluh-vay), X (eex), Y (ee-grek), Z (zed)

blocks.heading: Accent Aigu (é)
text: The acute accent - appears only on 'e' and makes it sound like 'ay'
{café}, {été} (summer), {déjà}

blocks.heading: {Accent Grave} ({è, à, ù})
text: The grave accent - on 'e' makes it sound like 'eh', on 'a' and 'u' it distinguishes meaning
{très}, {où} (where), {là} (there)

blocks.heading: Accent Circonflexe ({â, ê, î, ô, û})
text: The circumflex - can appear on any vowel, often indicates a historical 's' was dropped
{être} (to be), {hôtel}, {pâtes} (pasta), {île} (island)

blocks.heading: {Tréma} ({ë, ï, ü, ÿ})
text: The diaeresis - indicates two vowels are pronounced separately
{Noël} (Christmas), {naïve}, {maïs} (corn)

blocks.heading: {Cédille} (ç)
text: The cedilla - makes 'c' sound like 's' before a, o, u
{ça}, {français}, {garçon} (boy)

blocks.heading: Ligatures ({œ, æ})
text: Two letters merged together - œ is common, æ is rare
{cœur} (heart), {sœur} (sister), curriculum vitæ

words.note: feminine - a, e, i, o, u, y

blocks.heading: Numbers 0-20
text: The foundation numbers you need to memorize

{0 zéro}, {1 un}, {2 deux}, {3 trois}, {4 quatre}, {5 cinq}, {6 six}, {7 sept}, {8 huit}, {9 neuf}, {10 dix}, {11 onze}, {12 douze}, {13 treize}, {14 quatorze}, {15 quinze}, {16 seize}, {17 dix-sept}, {18 dix-huit}, {19 dix-neuf}, {20 vingt}

blocks.heading: Tens (20-60)
text: Regular tens that follow a pattern
{20 vingt}, {30 trente}, {40 quarante}, {50 cinquante}, {60 soixante}

blocks.heading: The Famous French 70s!
text: 70 = sixty-ten (soixante-dix). French counts: 71 (sixty-eleven), 72 (sixty-twelve), etc.
{70 soixante-dix}, {71 soixante-et-onze}, {75 soixante-quinze}, {79 soixante-dix-neuf}

blocks.heading: The Infamous French 80s!
text: 80 = four-twenties (quatre-vingts). A remnant of Celtic base-20 counting!
{80 quatre-vingts}, {81 quatre-vingt-un}, {85 quatre-vingt-cinq}, {89 quatre-vingt-neuf}

blocks.heading: The Wild French 90s!
text: 90 = four-twenty-ten (quatre-vingt-dix). Combining both systems!
{90 quatre-vingt-dix, 91 quatre-vingt-onze, 95 quatre-vingt-quinze, 99 quatre-vingt-dix-neuf}

blocks.heading: Numbers 21-69 Pattern
text: Add single digits with a hyphen. Use '{et}' (and) for 21, 31, 41, 51, 61
{21 vingt-et-un}, {22 vingt-deux}, {35 trente-cinq}, {47 quarante-sept}, {69 soixante-neuf}

blocks.heading: Large Numbers
text: Hundreds, thousands, millions - building bigger numbers
{100 cent}, {200 deux cents}, {1000 mille}, 1,000,{000 un million}, 1,000,000,{000 un milliard}

blocks.heading: Belgian & Swiss Variation
text: More logical! Belgium and Switzerland use: 70 septante, 90 nonante
70 septante (vs soixante-dix), 90 nonante (vs quatre-vingt-dix). Much easier!

blocks.heading: Important Exceptions & Rules
text: Key exceptions you need to know to avoid common mistakes

1) '{et}' (and) only for 21, 31, 41, 51, 61, 71 - NOT 81 or 91! 2) '{quatre-vingts}' (80) has 's' but '{quatre-vingt-un}' (81) loses it. 3) '{cents}' plural: '{deux cents}' (200) but '{deux cent un}' (201). 4) '{mille}' NEVER plural: '{trois mille}' (3,000) not 'milles'. 5) Hyphens between all parts EXCEPT before/after 'et' or '{cent}/{mille'}

blocks.heading: Days of the Week
text: Seven days - NEVER capitalized in French (unlike English!)
{lundi} (Monday), {mardi} (Tuesday), {mercredi} (Wednesday), {jeudi} (Thursday), {vendredi} (Friday), {samedi} (Saturday), {dimanche} (Sunday)

blocks.heading: Months of the Year
text: Twelve months - also NEVER capitalized in French
{janvier}, {février}, {mars}, {avril}, {mai}, {juin}, {juillet}, {août}, {septembre}, {octobre}, {novembre}, {décembre}

blocks.heading: Seasons ({Les Saisons})
text: Four seasons - note the articles!
{le printemps} (spring), {l'été} (summer), {l'automne} (fall), {l'hiver} (winter)

blocks.heading: Useful Time Phrases
text: Essential words for talking about days and time
{aujourd'hui} (today), {demain} (tomorrow), {hier} (yesterday), {cette semaine} (this week), {le week-end} (the weekend)

blocks.heading: {Les Jours Fériés} (National Holidays)
text: France has 11 official public holidays - more than most countries!
{le Nouvel An} (Jan 1), {Pâques} (Easter), {la Fête Nationale} (July 14 - Bastille Day), {Noël} (Dec 25)

blocks.heading: Bastille Day - {La Fête Nationale}
text: July 14 - France's most important holiday celebrating the French Revolution (1789)
{Military parade on Champs-Élysées, fireworks, parties} - like July 4th in America but with more cheese!

blocks.heading: Religious Holidays
text: France is secular but many Catholic holidays are still official days off
{Pâques} (Easter), Ascension, Pentecôte (Pentecost), Assomption (Aug 15), Toussaint (Nov 1 - All Saints)

blocks.heading: WWI & WWII Commemorations
text: France honors both world wars with official holidays
{8 mai} - {Victoire 1945} (WWII), {11 novembre} - Armistice 1918 (WWI)

blocks.heading: Fun French Traditions
text: Unique celebrations you won't find everywhere!
{la Chandeleur} (Feb 2 - Crêpe Day!), {le Poisson d'Avril} (April 1 - stick fish on backs!), {la Fête de la Musique} (June 21 - free concerts everywhere!)

blocks.heading: Christmas & New Year ({Les Réveillons})
text: Two huge celebrations with fancy dinners called '{réveillons}'
{le Réveillon de Noël} (Christmas Eve dinner), {le Réveillon du Nouvel An} (New Year's Eve), {la Galette des Rois} (Jan 6 - King Cake with hidden prize!)

blocks.heading: Quebec Holidays
text: French Canada has unique celebrations
{la Saint-Jean-Baptiste} (June 24 - Quebec National Day), {le Jour du Souvenir} (Nov 11 - Remembrance Day)

blocks.heading: Holiday Greetings
text: Essential phrases for celebrating
{Joyeux Noël!} (Merry Christmas!), {Bonne année!} (Happy New Year!), {Joyeuses Pâques!} (Happy Easter!), {Bon anniversaire!} (Happy Birthday!)

blocks.heading: Colors are Adjectives
text: In French, colors are adjectives that agree with the noun in gender and number. They usually come AFTER the noun.
{le ciel bleu} (the blue sky), {une maison blanche} (a white house), {des yeux verts} (green eyes)

blocks.heading: Basic Colors
text: The most common colors you'll use every day - memorize these first!
{bleu} (blue), {rouge} (red), {vert} (green), {jaune} (yellow), {blanc} (white), {noir} (black)

blocks.heading: Feminine Forms
text: Add -e to make most colors feminine. Some have special forms.
{bleu} → {bleue}, {vert} → {verte}, {blanc} → {blanche}, {rouge} → rouge (no change)

blocks.heading: Plural Forms
text: Add -s for plural (unless already ends in -s or -x)
{bleu} → {bleus} (masculine plural), {bleue} → {bleues} (feminine plural), {gris} → gris (no change)

blocks.heading: Invariable Colors
text: Some colors never change: marron (brown), orange (orange). These are actually nouns used as adjectives!
{un chat marron}, {une maison marron}, {des chats marron} (no -s!)

blocks.heading: Compound Colors
text: Colors with two words or modified colors are invariable (never change)
{des yeux bleu clair} (light blue eyes), {des robes bleu foncé} (dark blue dresses)

blocks.heading: Using Colors in Questions
text: Now you can ask about colors of things!
{De quelle couleur est le ciel?} (What color is the sky?) → {Le ciel est bleu. Pourquoi est-ce que l'herbe est verte?} (Why is grass green?)

blocks.heading: La Francophonie - The French-Speaking World
text: French is spoken by 300+ million people across 29 countries as an official language
5th most spoken language globally, 2nd most studied language, official language of UN, EU, NATO, Olympics

blocks.heading: {Europe} - Where It All Began
text: France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Monaco - 90 million French speakers
{France} (67M - birthplace), Belgium (11.5M - also Dutch/German), Switzerland (8.6M - also German/Italian), {Luxembourg} (632K), Monaco (39K)

blocks.heading: North America - Québec & Haiti
text: 8+ million French speakers, primarily in Quebec (Canada) and Haiti
Quebec (7.9M - '{Je me souviens}'), Haiti (11.4M - French + Creole), Louisiana (200K speakers), {Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon} (6K)

blocks.heading: Africa - The Future of French!
text: Africa has the MOST French speakers (60% of global total) and growing fast!
By 2050, 85% of French speakers will be in Africa. Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake France as #1 French-speaking country!

blocks.heading: West Africa - French Belt
text: 11 countries where French is the official language
Senegal (16M), {Côte d'Ivoire} (26M - economic hub), Mali (20M), Burkina Faso (21M), Niger (24M), Benin (12M), Togo (8M), Guinea (13M)

blocks.heading: Central Africa - Congo Basin
text: French is the lingua franca connecting hundreds of ethnic groups
DRC (90M - 2nd largest!), Cameroon (27M - also English), Chad (16M), Congo-Brazzaville (5.5M), {CAR} (4.8M), Gabon (2.2M)

blocks.heading: North Africa - Le Maghreb
text: French widely spoken alongside Arabic in former French colonies
Morocco (33% speak French), Algeria (33%), Tunisia (66%) - French used in business, education, media

blocks.heading: East Africa & Islands
text: French official in 7 countries and island nations
Madagascar (28M), Rwanda (13M), Burundi (12M), Djibouti (990K), Comoros (870K), Seychelles (98K), Mauritius (1.3M)

blocks.heading: Caribbean - Les Antilles
text: French departments and territories in the Caribbean
Guadeloupe (400K), Martinique (375K), French Guiana (290K) - all part of France with euros and French laws!

blocks.heading: Middle East & Asia
text: Former French influence still present
Lebanon (40% speak French - Paris of Middle East), Vietnam (600K - legacy of French Indochina)

blocks.heading: Pacific Islands - {Polynésie Française}
text: French territories across the Pacific Ocean
French Polynesia/Tahiti (280K), New Caledonia (271K), Vanuatu (307K - French, English, Bislama official)

blocks.heading: The Future is African!
text: By 2050, French will have 700 million speakers - mostly due to African population growth
DRC will have more French speakers than France! French will be Africa's most-spoken language. 85% of French speakers will be African.

blocks.heading: French Sounds - Phonology
text: French has 36-37 distinct sounds (phonemes) - 16 vowels and 20-21 consonants
4 nasal vowels (ã, ẽ, õ, {œ̃}) - unique to French! No 'th' sound (why 'the' is hard). Uvular 'r' (back of throat).

blocks.heading: Syllable-Timed Language
text: Each syllable gets equal time - unlike English which stresses certain words
French flows smoothly with even rhythm. No word stress like English! Emphasis on last syllable of phrases. Creates musical, flowing sound.

blocks.heading: Speaking Speed
text: French speakers talk fast! 7.0-8.0 syllables per second vs English 6.5
French needs more syllables to convey same info (lower information density), so speakers compensate by speaking faster!

blocks.heading: The Alphabet & Accents
text: 26 letters + 5 diacritical marks + 2 ligatures
Letters: same as English. Accents: {é è ê ë à ù û ç. Ligatures}: œ ({cœur}), æ ({rare}). {Total}: {33 unique characters!}

blocks.heading: Vocabulary Size
text: 100,000 words in common use - educated speakers know 30,000 actively
{Le Grand Robert dictionary}: 100,000 words, 350,000 definitions. Average person: 5,000-30,000 words depending on education.

blocks.heading: French Influence on English
text: 29% of English vocabulary comes from French (thanks to Norman Conquest 1066!)
45% of English has Latin/French origins total. Beef, pork, royal, justice, parliament - all from French!

blocks.heading: Grammar Complexity
text: 2 genders, 17-20 verb tenses, ~350 irregular verbs (only ~50 common)
Masculine/Feminine. 3 verb groups (-er, -ir, -re) + irregulars. ~25 '{essential}' irregular verbs to memorize. SVO word order like English.

blocks.heading: Global Ranking
text: 5th most spoken, 2nd most studied, 3rd language of business
300M speakers (2023), projected 700M by 2050. Official in 29 countries. One of 6 UN languages. Growing fast in Africa!

blocks.heading: Fun Language Facts
text: Quirky and interesting trivia about French
Longest word: '{anticonstitutionnellement}' (25 letters). Most common word: '{de}'. Most common letter: 'e' (15%). No word for 'home' or '{shallow}'!

blocks.heading: Liaison & Flow
text: Words link together smoothly - consonants connect to following vowels
'{les enfants}' sounds like 'lay-zahn-fahn' (z sound links). '{un homme}' = '{uh-nom}'. Creates beautiful flowing speech!

blocks.heading: {L'Académie Française}
text: Official authority on French language since 1635 - protects '{purity}' of French
40 immortals (lifetime members) decide official French. Resist English words. Prefer '{ordinateur}' to '{computer}', '{courriel}' to '{email}'.

blocks.heading: Perfect French Pangram
text: A sentence using all 26 letters
'{Portez ce vieux whisky au juge blond qui fume}' (Bring this old whisky to the blonde judge who smokes)

blocks.heading: French Pronunciation Patterns
text: French has unique sounds that differ from English
The French 'r' is guttural, vowels are pure, and many final consonants are silent

blocks.heading: Nasal Vowels
text: French has four nasal vowel sounds not found in English
Words like '{bon}', '{un}', '{vin}', and '{pain}' use nasal vowels

blocks.heading: Liaison and Elision
text: French words flow together in speech
Silent consonants become pronounced when followed by vowels, like 'les amis' (lay-za-mee)

blocks.heading: Saying hello
text: {ça va ?} and {comment ça va ?} ask how someone is, and {ça va} answers.
{Salut, ça va ? Oui, ça va bien.}

blocks.heading: Being polite
text: Use {excusez-moi} to get someone's attention, {je voudrais} to ask for something, and {s'il te plaît} or {s'il vous plaît} to say please.
{Excusez-moi, je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.}

blocks.heading: In conversation
text: You will hear these often in everyday conversation: {bien sûr}, {de temps en temps}, {quelque chose}, {tout le monde} and {n'est-ce pas}.
{Tout le monde aime le chocolat, n'est-ce pas ?}

words.example_en: Hi, how's it going? Yes, it's going well.

words.meaning_en: how's it going? / it's going fine

words.example_en: Excuse me, where is the station?

words.example_fr: Passe-moi le pain, s'il te plaît.
words.note: To someone you call {vous}, say {s'il vous plaît}.

words.example_en: I would like a croissant, please.

words.note: Use it to ask politely for something in a shop or café.

words.example_en: Are you coming tonight? Of course!

words.example_en: I go to the cinema from time to time.

words.example_en: Do you want something to drink?
words.example_fr: Tu veux quelque chose à boire ?
words.note: Before an adjective, add {de}: {quelque chose de bon}.
It takes the {il} form of the verb: {tout le monde est là}.

words.example_en: The weather is nice, isn't it?
words.note: Put it at the end of a sentence to ask someone to agree.
